title: How to ask for an NHS interpreter in England
summary: How to ask for an interpreter at a GP practice or hospital or when you call NHS 111, and what to do if support has not been arranged.
content:
# How to ask for an NHS interpreter in England

Last updated: 2026-11-27

> This guide covers **England**. Arrangements are different in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and we will cover them separately.

Many people have enough English for the supermarket or asking for directions. Seeing a doctor is different: you need to explain clearly where it hurts, how long it has hurt, what medicines you take and what illnesses you have had before. In many families, parents speak no English at all and rely on their children to translate.

This guide explains how to ask for an interpreter when you see a doctor in England, who arranges it, whether you have to pay, and whether family members should really be interpreting for you.

An **interpreter** helps people communicate during a conversation. **Translation** is for written documents. This Guide covers the interpretation you can request at the appointment or by phone.

## Seeing a GP: say you need an interpreter when you book

When booking a GP appointment, ask for an interpreter and say which language you need. NHS England's primary-care guidance explains how to ask for language support when booking. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-request-interpreter-when-booking)

Many people manage everyday English but not medical English. In that case you can also explain to the practice that you need an interpreter to describe your symptoms clearly and understand what you are told.

NHS England's interpreting guidance for primary care, such as GP services, is quite specific:

- interpreting should be free at the point of use: **patients should not be charged, and should not be asked to bring their own interpreter**;
- when an interpreter is needed, **the practice is responsible for booking one**;
- interpreters must be registered with an appropriate regulator and should be familiar with medical terms;
- appointments with an interpreter usually take longer; the guidance says typically about twice as long as a regular appointment;
- your language needs should be recorded in your notes and passed on when you are referred to hospital;
- interpreting can be face to face, by phone or by video, and the practice should tell you which options are available;
- you can say if you prefer an interpreter of a particular gender. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-primary-care-interpreting-principles)

This is NHS England guidance for the organisations that commission GP services, and most of it says "should". The guidance also accepts that getting a suitable interpreter in time depends on local availability. So if arrangements are difficult, you can use these principles when talking to the practice, but do not take them to mean that an interpreter can always be arranged straight away. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-interpreter-availability-caveat)

## Tell staff which language you need

When you call the practice reception, you can simply say:

“I need an interpreter for my appointment. I speak [say your language or dialect].” Tell the practice whether the same arrangements are needed for a telephone or a video appointment.

Name your preferred spoken language and dialect, if relevant. Ask when and how the interpreter can join. Provision for a particular language, dialect or appointment can vary. You can ask your practice to record your language needs for future appointments.

## Can a family member interpret?

In many families, adult children or a spouse interpret for parents. NHS England's guidance says:

- patients should **always be offered a registered, professional interpreter**;
- relying on family, friends or unqualified people to interpret is **strongly discouraged** and not seen as good practice;
- if a patient clearly wants a family member or friend to interpret, their consent should be confirmed in their own language, separately from that family member or friend, and recorded in their notes. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-family-and-friends-as-interpreters)

In other words, the rules do not ban family members from interpreting, but a professional interpreter is preferred; if you choose a family member yourself, the practice should first check separately that this is really what you want.

There are practical reasons too. Appointments often involve very personal matters, and some things are hard to say in front of your children. However good a relative's English is, they may not know medical terms, and one wrong word can change the meaning a lot. If there are things you do not want your family to know, you can ask for a professional interpreter.

## Children should not interpret

In some families the child has the best English, so a teenager goes along to appointments and interprets for their parents throughout.

NHS England's guidance is very firm on this: **using anyone under 16 as an interpreter is not acceptable in any circumstance other than when immediate and necessary treatment is required**, and even then it should be an exception, because of safeguarding and the child's capacity. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-under-16-interpreters)

So however good a child's English is, it is best not to have them interpret for their parents in the consulting room.

## What about calling NHS 111?

Call 111 and ask for an interpreter. Tell the call handler which language you need. For example, say “Interpreter, please. I speak [your language].” [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-111-language-support)

111 also has an online service (111.nhs.uk). If you need an interpreter, you can ask for one directly when you call.

For people with hearing or speech difficulties, the NHS website also lists other ways to contact 111: call 18001 111 using text relay, or use the NHS 111 British Sign Language (BSL) video service. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-111-language-support)

## What about hospitals and A&E?

For hospitals, the evidence we found is less specific than for GPs:

- NHS England's interpreting guidance is written mainly for primary care such as GP services, but it says its contents may also apply to hospital sites; [See the official source](#guide-evidence-hospital-interpreting)
- the guidance also says your language needs should be recorded in your GP notes and **passed on when you are referred to hospital**;
- Healthwatch England, the statutory body that represents patients' views, says patients can ask for a professional interpreter at every stage of their care and should never have to pay for it. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-hospital-interpreting)

Each hospital has its own arrangements. For outpatient appointments, it is best to call the hospital in advance and tell them which language you need an interpreter for, and to mention it again at reception when you arrive.

For a life-threatening emergency, call 999. Do not delay getting emergency help because of a language barrier. Tell hospital staff which language you need as soon as you can. The hospital can explain its arrangements.

## You arrive and no interpreter has been arranged

This does happen sometimes. You can calmly explain that you asked for an interpreter when you booked, and ask whether they can use a telephone interpreter. Under the guidance, the practice is responsible for arranging interpreting and should not ask you to bring someone to interpret; the guidance also accepts that interpreters are not always available, so sometimes the appointment may need to be rearranged. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-interpreter-not-arranged)

If your condition is urgent, do not let waiting for an interpreter delay things: tell the staff straight away that it is urgent.

## Things to prepare before an appointment

- Tell your GP practice which language you need and remind staff when you book;
- remind them each time you book;
- write down your symptoms, medicines and allergies in the language you are most comfortable using;
- if there are things you do not want your family to know, ask for a professional interpreter rather than a family member;
- do not let children under 16 interpret for you.

## Official sources

All of the sources below were accessed on 5 October 2026.

- NHS England — *Guidance for commissioners: Interpreting and Translation Services in Primary Care* — https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/guidance-for-commissioners-interpreting-and-translation-services-in-primary-care.pdf
- NHS (NHS.uk) — *When to use 111* — https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/urgent-and-emergency-care-services/when-to-use-111/
- Healthwatch England — *Does the NHS provide an interpreter?* — https://www.healthwatch.co.uk/advice-and-information/2025-07-02/does-nhs-provide-interpreter
